title: 1947 Avianca Douglas DC-4 crash
summary: Douglas DC-4 C-114 crashed into a mountain two hours into a scheduled domestic flight from Ernesto Cortissoz International Airport to Techo International Airport in Colombia. The aircraft was carrying 49 passengers and 4 crew members including captain Kenneth Newton Poe and first officer Roy Kaye, with all 53 occupants killed.

factors.evidence: crashed into a mountain two hours into its flight, killing all 53 occupants on board

events.text: An Avianca Douglas DC-4 registered as C-114, powered by four Pratt & Whitney R-2000 Twin Wasp engines, operated a scheduled domestic passenger flight from Ernesto Cortissoz International Airport to Techo International Airport, Colombia.
The aircraft crashed into a mountain two hours into its flight, killing all 53 occupants on board.

notes: Text contains background information but no investigative detail about accident cause; richness floors waived due to sparse causal content

title: United Airlines 521
summary: United Air Lines Flight 521, a Douglas DC-4 from LaGuardia Airport, failed to become airborne on 29 May 1947 while attempting takeoff on runway 18. The aircraft overran the end of the runway, ripped through the airport fence onto traffic on the Grand Central Parkway, and slammed into an embankment before plunging into a pond and exploding. Ten people escaped the flaming wreckage; only five survived. It was the worst commercial aviation disaster in United States history at the time.
probable_cause: The Civil Aeronautics Board determined the probable cause was either the failure of the pilot to release the gust lock before takeoff, or the decision to discontinue the takeoff because of apprehension resulting from rapid use of a short runway under calm wind conditions. Initial reports suggested wind shear may have been a factor, with a wind shift of almost unbelievable suddenness occurring during takeoff.

factors.evidence: Aircraft used about two-thirds of the 3,500-foot runway during takeoff attempt
Wind shift described as of almost unbelievable suddenness led captain to decide against proceeding with takeoff
Aircraft overran the end of the runway after using about two-thirds of its length
Aircraft ripped through airport fence, slammed into embankment, plunged into pond and exploded

events.text: Aircraft positioned on runway 18 at LaGuardia Airport for takeoff to Cleveland
Wind shift of almost unbelievable suddenness occurred during takeoff roll
Captain Benton R. Baldwin decided to discontinue takeoff after using about two-thirds of 3,500-foot runway; applied brakes attempting to halt giant craft by braking and ground looping
Aircraft overran end of runway, ripped through airport fence onto Grand Central Parkway traffic, slammed into embankment and plunged into pond
Aircraft exploded in pond with flames and wreckage; ten people escaped but only five survived

notes: CAB concluded probable cause was pilot error but initial reports suggested windshear
Captain Baldwin's decision-making disputed between board and press reports
May have been gust lock failure but uncertainty reflected in probable cause statement
Worst commercial aviation disaster in US history at the time
Record lasted less than 24 hours before Eastern Air Lines DC-4 crash near Baltimore killed 53

title: Pennsylvania Central Airlines 410
summary: Pennsylvania Central Airlines Flight 410, a Douglas DC-4, crashed into Lookout Rock in the West Virginia Blue Ridge Mountains at approximately 1,425 feet elevation while descending for Washington DC. All 50 passengers and crew were killed. The aircraft encountered thunderstorm weather, and the crew requested an alternate route requiring descent from 7,000 to 2,500 feet. The investigation found the pilot had erred in descending below the minimum altitude without adequate visual references and that ATC and the dispatcher provided an inappropriate clearance for an airway without established minimum altitude.
probable_cause: The pilot had erred in descending below the minimum altitude for which the flight had received clearance without adequate ground references. Contributing fault was assigned to Airway Traffic Control and the PCA dispatcher for providing an inappropriate clearance.

factors.evidence: aircraft encountered a thunderstorm on the leg from Chicago to Cleveland
aircraft was informed of air traffic delays and deteriorating weather conditions
pilot radioed in their position at 1,000-foot increments from 7,000 feet to 3,000 feet and then struck a ridge at elevation of approximately 1,425 feet
Airway 61 Red was only recently approved by CAA for PCA but no minimum altitude had been set
aircraft struck a ridge in the Blue Ridge Mountains approximately two miles east of Shenandoah River

events.text: Flight 410 radioed position at 7,000 feet approaching Washington with air traffic delays and deteriorating weather reported
Pilot requested alternate approach route requiring descent from 7,000 to 2,500 feet
Flight 410 radioed position at 3,000 feet with Washington reported only 20 minutes flying time away
Aircraft struck a ridge in the Blue Ridge Mountains at elevation of 1,425 feet

title: United Air Lines 608
summary: In-flight fire in the baggage compartment developed from overfilled fuel tank venting into the cabin heater system. As the aircraft descended toward Bryce Canyon Airport, pieces of the aircraft including the right wing fell off. The crew was unable to maintain control in canyon gusts despite being only 10 feet above ground, and the aircraft crashed on National Park Service land. The fire and structural damage resulted from a design flaw in the cabin heater intake scoop placement relative to the fuel tank vent.
probable_cause: Design flaw: a cabin heater intake scoop was positioned too close to the number 3 alternate fuel tank air vent. When the fuel tank was overfilled during routine transfer, excess fuel was sucked into the cabin heater system and ignited. Contributing factors were inadequate crew training about the danger and failure to halt the fuel transfer before tank overflow.

factors.evidence: fuel flowed out of the tank vent after overfilling during fuel transfer between wing tanks
the excess fuel sucked into the cabin heater system ignited, causing fire in the baggage compartment
pieces of the airplane including portions of the right wing started to fall off
cabin heater intake scoop was positioned too close to the number 3 alternate fuel tank air vent
inadequate training of the crew about the danger

events.text: United Air Lines Flight 608 departed from Los Angeles at 10:23 am and climbed to 19,000 feet
Fuel overfilled during transfer between wing tanks, excess fuel venting from number 3 alternate fuel tank
Captain Everett L. McMillen radioed that fire was in the baggage compartment with smoke entering passenger cabin
Aircraft descended toward Bryce Canyon, pieces including right wing fell off and emergency flare on wing ignited
Occupants threw items from cabin door in attempt to lighten load as DC-6 descended over canyon
Crippled aircraft only 10 feet off ground pulled out of control by canyon gusts and crashed on National Park Service land

notes: First crash of a DC-6 aircraft type
Similar incident with American Airlines DC-6 at Gallup landing safely allowed investigation of intact aircraft
Entire DC-6 fleet grounded and recalled after accident; design changes persist today
